SEED: de2b3ef57c54029fa748855d418b35fc

AXIS: Statistical rigour
STANCE: Maximally adversarial

(Note: the arXiv lookup tool returned a persistent proxy/connection error on two queries; per the fallback rule I am proceeding from the paper text alone, and no external citations appear below that were not already in the manuscript's own reference list.)

---

# Review — Reviewer alfa

## Summary

The thesis makes three linked claims: (1) a large fraction (76%) of handovers in the authors' own one-hertz LTE drive-test export are mislabeled by an end-of-second aggregation artifact, and correcting it collapses a headline AUPRC from 0.600 to 0.179; (2) a discrete-time hazard formulation predicts the next handover with modest skill (AUPRC 0.179 at 1s, 2.6× the prevalence floor; AUROC 0.777) while guaranteeing monotonic multi-horizon probabilities by construction; and (3) a distribution-free conformal risk bound on "miss rate" is reported honestly as failing to hold under cross-campaign deployment and as inexpressible at the 1s horizon for over a third of events. The alignment-audit finding (1) is genuinely valuable and unusually well-instrumented — it is corroborated on an independent multi-operator corpus and falsified against a public log with a different sampling mechanism. However, on close inspection the statistical apparatus behind claims (2) and (3) is applied inconsistently: the authors correctly diagnose, in one place, that their own 180-second block-bootstrap manufactures anti-conservative confidence intervals because blocks within a campaign are not independent — and withdraw a specific claim on that basis — but they do not apply the same skepticism to the primary AUPRC intervals or to the "exchangeable regime" conformal result that use the identical resampling machinery. With only n=4 truly independent units (campaigns) throughout, and per-campaign AUPRC spreads (0.132–0.233) wide enough to swallow the reported "2.6× lift," the headline predictive numbers should be read as far less precise than the tables imply. My overall stance: this is an unusually self-critical thesis with one strong contribution (the alignment audit) and a predictive/statistical contribution whose reported precision does not survive the paper's own logic applied consistently.

## Major concerns

1. **Issue** — The single largest correction in the thesis (the one-row alignment lag) was discovered by inspecting all four campaigns, including the campaign later reported as a held-out generalization test, which undermines the generalization claim built on it. `[Evidence — pre-registration/post-hoc]`
   **Where** — Section 3.2 ("the alignment audit of Section 5.1 ... was performed after all four campaigns, so no campaign is out of sample with respect to it"); Section 5.6 / Table 5.10 (leave-one-campaign-out results, including the "held-out" 4th/highway campaign).
   **Why it matters** — Objective O4 and Section 5.6 present the 4th campaign as a genuine out-of-distribution test of corridor and speed regime. But the feature-construction methodology itself (the lag, and by extension the entire feature pipeline that replaced the leaky one) was tuned using that same campaign's data before ever being "held out" for model evaluation. What survives as a clean LOCO test is only the model's hyperparameters, not the measurement/feature pipeline that determines what the model sees. This is exactly the class of leakage the thesis spends Section 5.1 teaching the reader to distrust (leakage into training examples that "every syntactic check passes"), applied one level up, to methodology rather than features.
   **What would address it** — Explicitly reframe the O4 claim as "the model generalizes across corridors given a feature pipeline validated on all available data" rather than "the system generalizes to a held-out corridor," or obtain a fifth campaign collected and audited without ever being used to shape the pipeline.

2. **Issue** — No hyperparameter search space, network depth/width, or learning-rate range is given anywhere for the five non-tree learners (logistic regression aside), so the headline numbers cannot be independently reproduced from the text alone. `[Reproducibility]`
   **Where** — Section 4.7 ("Models compared") and Section 4.9 ("twenty random-search trials per outer fold") — no table of search bounds for MLP, TCN, Transformer, or GRU appears in the main text or Appendix B/C.
   **Why it matters** — Reproduction Notes (Appendix C) describes a pipeline of "numbered stages" and a "manifest," but that manifest is not shown, and code/data are only "committed on acceptance" — a promise with no defined venue or deadline attached here. A reader cannot check whether the reported AUPRC of 0.179 depends on a search space that happened to favor LightGBM, nor replicate Table 5.5's near-tie among seven learners.
   **What would address it** — Publish the actual search spaces (as a table) alongside the manuscript, not deferred to a hypothetical "acceptance."

3. **Issue** — The central falsification test for the aggregation-mechanism hypothesis relies on n=15 cases, and "0 of 15 contaminated" is reported with more confidence than that sample size supports. `[Evidence — statistical rigour, small-n]`
   **Where** — Section 5.1: "of the 15 handovers whose diagnostic completion interval crosses the boundary contaminates its row" / "an empirical hypothesis falsified by none of the 15 handovers here."
   **Why it matters** — If the true contamination rate in this regime were, say, 15%, the probability of observing zero contaminated cases in 15 trials by chance is still ≈0.87^15 ≈ 10%, i.e., not strong evidence of a hard zero. The same caution applies to the "isolated handovers" subsample (n=291) used to compute several downstream percentages (e.g., Table 5.1's "isolated" row), and to the fine-grained margin bins later in the same section (e.g., "903 handovers... 98.2% when 75 to 100 ms remain") where per-sub-bin counts are never stated, so the precision of the inferred "~60ms" logging-delay estimate cannot be assessed.
   **What would address it** — Report per-bin sample sizes for every contamination percentage in Section 5.1, and attach a confidence interval (even a simple Wilson interval) to the "0/15" and "60ms cliff" claims rather than presenting them as exact.

4. **Issue** — The claim that "no wireless conformal study ... reports a mobility-management case" rests on an unspecified literature screen with no stated search protocol, term list, or paper count — unlike the well-documented 108→22 screen used for the handover-prediction audit in Section 2.3. `[Novelty]`
   **Where** — Section 2.6 ("no wireless conformal study located in three screening passes reports a mobility-management case at all") and the parallel sentence in Section 2.9.
   **Why it matters** — This is exactly the kind of unverifiable negative-existence claim the paper otherwise takes pains to avoid (it audits the handover-prediction literature with a transparent, gradeable table). Readers cannot tell whether "three screening passes" means three keyword searches or three exhaustive database sweeps, so the strength of the "no prior mobility-management conformal work" claim — which underwrites part of contribution #5 — cannot be assessed independently.
   **What would address it** — Apply the same audit discipline used in Table 2.1/Section 2.3 to the conformal-prediction-in-wireless literature: state the search terms, date range, and paper count screened.

5. **Issue** — The thesis proves, in one place, that its own 180-second block-bootstrap produces anti-conservative confidence intervals due to intra-campaign correlation, and withdraws a claim on that basis — but continues to report and lean on statistically identical intervals, unflagged with the same caveat, for its two most important quantitative results: the primary AUPRC figure and the "exchangeable regime" conformal risk-control success. `[Evidence — statistical rigour]`
   **Where** — Section 5.4: "That version bootstrapped the paired differences over 180-second blocks ... Section 5.3 of this same thesis proves those blocks are not independent — splitting on them inflates one-second AUPRC by 13% — so resampling them deflates the standard error and manufactures a confidence interval narrower than the evidence supports. The claim is withdrawn." Contrast with Table 5.4's caption ("Intervals are block-bootstrapped over 180s blocks") reporting AUPRC 0.179 [0.159, 0.204] at 1s, and with Section 5.5's "exchangeable reference regime" (57 pooled 180-second blocks, calibration n≈43) reporting a successful conformal bound (realized loss 0.168 at α=0.20) using the same block-level resampling that Section 5.3 independently showed inflates apparent performance by 13% when used for model splitting.
   **Why it matters** — This is not a hypothetical concern; the paper's own Section 5.3 experiment (identical data, identical folds, only the splitting/resampling unit varied) is the direct evidence that 180-second blocks share enough structure (cells, traffic, trajectory) to bias any interval built from resampling them. The primary claim of the thesis — "AUPRC 0.179 at one second... against 0.116 for the A3 signal-margin proxy" — is defended with an interval built from exactly the mechanism the authors elsewhere call out as anti-conservative. The per-campaign spread the authors do report honestly (Table 5.10: AUPRC 0.132 to 0.233 across the four held-out campaigns) is wide enough that a properly cluster-aware (n=4) interval would very plausibly overlap the A3-proxy baseline and would certainly be far wider than [0.159, 0.204]. Likewise, the "exchangeable regime" conformal success in Section 5.5 is exactly the kind of within-corpus, block-level exchangeability the paper's own splitting-ladder experiment discredits as a proxy for genuine independence; labeling it "exchangeable" and reporting it as meeting the target (0.168 ≤ 0.20) risks being read as "conformal risk control worked here" when the same logic that invalidated Table 5.8's comparison applies with equal force.
   **What would address it** — Either (a) recompute the primary AUPRC/ECE intervals and the "exchangeable regime" conformal bound using a resampling unit the paper itself considers defensible (i.e., the 4 campaigns, accepting that this yields uninformative or very wide intervals, as the paper already does for paired-difference tests), or (b) attach to Table 5.4, Table 5.5, and Section 5.5 the same explicit anti-conservatism caveat given to Table 5.8, rather than the softer "conditional on these four sessions" hedge currently used only for the headline numbers.

## Minor concerns

- The reference list contains multiple unresolved bibliographic TODOs at the time of this text — e.g., ref [38] ("confirm the version DOI before submission"), [6] and [15] ("author list to be completed"), [39] ("venue to be confirmed"), [43]/[44] ("volume, issue and page range to be confirmed") — and [38] is the dataset underlying the Section 5.7 "independent collection" generalization claim, so its exact version is not yet pinned down.
- Figure 5.3's caption ("LightGBM consistently achieves the highest lift") is in tension with the body text's explicit disclaimer two pages later that "the ordering of the top arms is not a finding of this thesis" (Section 5.2) — a skimming reader would come away with the opposite conclusion from the one the authors intend.
- Table 5.9's formatting embeds a footnoted asterisk directly into a data cell ("100%*0%"), and reports a degenerate operating point (λ=0, 100% alarm rate, "0% realised loss") in a results table without strongly marking it as vacuous — it is flagged in a footnote but easy to miss.
- Handover counts (957, 938, 935, 934) recur across chapters with slightly different denominators depending on quality-control stage; a single master reconciliation table (analogous to Appendix B.1's feature-count table) would remove the need to re-derive which N applies where.
- Equation (4.8)'s claim about which horizon suffers the larger distortion under class reweighting ("largest at the shortest horizon" vs "largest at the longest") is a first-order approximation for small λ, presented with more confidence than the derivation supports, and is never checked empirically.
- Chapter 6 (Outcome-Based Education / course-outcome mapping) is program-accreditation boilerplate that would need to be removed entirely before any journal submission; worth flagging given the stated goal of the surrounding project.
- Checks that produced nothing of note: cherry-picking (Table 5.18/Figure 5.20's nine cases are explicitly drawn uniformly at random with a fixed seed — good practice, not cherry-picked); baseline strength (the A3 signal-margin proxy and the domain-adaptation baselines appear to have been implemented in reasonably good faith, and the CORAL null result is consistent with the cited benchmarking literature); competing-interest disclosure (Section 6.6 discloses the supervisor's co-authorship of the "independent" dataset and comparator plainly, and appropriately downgrades the word "independent").

## Belief update

I updated moderately on one specific, narrow proposition: *published drive-test handover-prediction accuracy figures built on one-hertz aggregate exports are at meaningful risk of being inflated by an aggregation-boundary labeling artifact that standard grouped-split leakage checks do not catch.* The magnitude here (AUPRC 0.600 → 0.179, a 3.4× collapse) and the cross-instrument corroboration (the NUWiNS downsample-both-ways test) make this a credible, generalizable methodological finding independent of everything else in the thesis. I did not update toward believing that the discrete-time hazard formulation or the conformal risk-control machinery add practical value here: the hazard model does not outrank the free monotone-projection controls, the conformal bound is explicitly not established cross-campaign, and I now trust the headline AUPRC number itself less than the tables suggest, given finding #5 above.

## Verdict

**Major revision.** The alignment-audit contribution is strong and worth publishing, but the primary predictive and risk-control numbers are defended with confidence intervals the paper's own Section 5.3 analysis shows to be anti-conservative when applied to this data's block structure — that inconsistency (Major concern #5) must be resolved, and the headline AUPRC/conformal claims re-expressed with honest n=4-cluster uncertainty, before the quantitative claims can be taken at face value.

SEED: 8f3ac9d21b74e605fa2d9c3b7e14f860

LENS: Experimental design (controls, confounds, blinding, pre-registration)
STANCE: Adversarial (assume the headline result is false; what would falsify it?)

### Summary
This thesis asks whether the next LTE handover can be forecast ahead of the reactive Event A3 trigger, using four drive-test campaigns (4 continuous sessions, 10,260 one-hertz samples, 957 RRC-signalling-confirmed handover commands) on a single commercial operator. Its most consequential finding is methodological rather than predictive: a timestamp-alignment audit shows that in 76% of handovers the one-hertz export row stamped just before the command already reflects the post-handover serving cell, so an uncorrected model's apparent one-second AUPRC of 0.600 collapses to 0.179 once every export feature is lagged by one row. Under a discrete-time hazard formulation evaluated by leave-one-campaign-out cross-validation, gradient-boosted trees reach AUPRC 0.179 (2.6× lift, AUROC 0.777) at one second and 0.475 (1.8×) at five seconds, modestly ahead of an implemented A3 signal-margin proxy (AUPRC 0.116). The paper also reports a distribution-free (conformal) risk bound that is descriptive rather than certified across campaigns, corrects two prior characterisations of the deployed A3 configuration, and documents several negative results, explicitly framing its contribution as the leakage-audited measurement framework rather than a deployable predictor.

### Major concerns

1. **Issue** — The single most consequential analytic decision (the one-row lag and which feature columns to lag) was derived by inspecting contamination evidence pooled across *all four* campaigns, including the campaign that the leave-one-campaign-out protocol treats as "held out," so the generalization claim is not a blind test of the finished pipeline.
   **Where** — Section 3.2 ("the alignment audit of Section 5.1 … was performed after all four campaigns, so no campaign is out of sample with respect to it"); Section 5.1 (the audit pools evidence across the whole corpus to establish the end-of-second mechanism and the one-row rule); Objective O4 and Section 5.6.
   **Why it matters** — The paper's rhetorical structure treats Campaign 4 as an experimental control ("driven after the modelling decisions… had been recorded," "the only campaign that differs in both corridor and speed regime, so it is reported as a held-out campaign throughout"). But the feature-construction rule actually applied to Campaign 4 during evaluation (lag every export column) was chosen using contamination statistics that included Campaign 4 itself. This is a design leak at the level of pipeline construction, not row-level leakage — exactly the "leakage in training examples" category the paper itself invokes (via Kaufman et al.) to describe the original defect it found. A skeptic should ask: would the audit have concluded "lag by exactly one row" if only Campaigns 1–3 had been available? The paper does not show this, so the reported LOCO numbers for Campaign 4 cannot be cleanly attributed to genuine generalization.
   **What would address it** — Re-derive the alignment/lag rule using only Campaigns 1–3, freeze it, and then apply it unmodified to Campaign 4 as a genuinely blind test; report whether the audit's conclusions and the resulting AUPRC/AUROC figures for Campaign 4 change.

2. **Issue** — The "freeze" of modelling decisions before Campaign 4 was collected is attested only by the authors' own private version history, not by any independently verifiable timestamp.
   **Where** — Section 3.2: "The freeze was recorded in the project's own version history between the 3rd and 4th Campaigns in 2026, not registered with a third party, so it is auditable but not independently timestamped."
   **Why it matters** — The credibility of every "held-out campaign" claim in the paper rests on trusting that the feature set, model family, and evaluation protocol genuinely did not change after seeing Campaign 4. Given how many numbers in this same thesis are explicitly flagged as revisions of an "earlier draft" that got things wrong (the report-conversion rate, the offset-weighting claim, the compounding-error argument, the ping-pong lever claim, the omission of monotone-projection controls), the base rate of analytic revision in this project is high. Without third-party registration, a reviewer cannot rule out that the "freeze" itself was adjusted retrospectively along with everything else.
   **What would address it** — Use an external, timestamped registration mechanism (e.g., a signed commit hash lodged with the supervisor or an OSF pre-registration) for any future confirmatory claim of this kind.

3. **Issue** — The claim of generalisation "across corridors and speed regimes" (Objective O4) is drawn from a single campaign in which corridor, speed, carrier mix, cell density, and time-of-day all covary, so no factor can be attributed the observed change in performance.
   **Where** — Section 3.2 (Campaign 4 "differs in both corridor and speed regime"); Section 5.10 explicitly concedes the same confound for the ping-pong analysis ("with one campaign per regime, speed is completely confounded with route, cell density, carrier mix and time of day"); Objective O4 in Section 1.4.
   **Why it matters** — A held-out session that differs simultaneously along every axis is a test of "does the model transfer to this one other bundle of conditions," not a test of speed-regime generalisation specifically. The paper's own Section 5.10 admits this for ping-pong but does not carry the same caution into the framing of O4's "success," where AUROC 0.765–0.805 across four held-out campaigns is presented as evidence the result "generalises... to a corridor and speed regime held out entirely."
   **What would address it** — A minimal 2×2 design (same corridor at two speeds; two corridors at matched speed) before any claim naming speed regime specifically as a validated axis of generalisation.

4. **Issue** — The cross-campaign conformal risk-control result reports "12 individual rotations" as if they were 12 independent trials, when they are pseudo-replicated draws from only 4 independent campaigns.
   **Where** — Section 5.5 and Table 5.9: "empirical holdout loss falling below α in 83% of 12 individual rotations."
   **Why it matters** — With 4 campaigns, calibrate-on-one/test-on-another rotations number at most 12, but each campaign contributes to multiple rotations (as calibration set in some, test set in others), so the 12 outcomes are correlated through shared campaign identity. A single unusually favourable or unfavourable campaign can dominate several of the 12 "successes/failures," making 83% look more robust than 4 independent data points can support — precisely the kind of statistical over-counting the paper is careful to avoid everywhere else (e.g., its explicit refusal to run a sign test with n=4).
   **What would address it** — Report the 12 outcomes grouped by which campaign served as the test set, and state plainly that the effective sample size for this claim is 4, consistent with the paper's own standard elsewhere.

5. **Issue** — Two of the three external-validity checks (the "independent" public dataset and the RL comparator) are not independent of the authors' own research lineage, and this is only partly reflected in how the results are framed.
   **Where** — Section 5.7 ("collected by a different group of people... using the same operator, the same city, and the same XCAL licence, in the same department of the same institution"); Section 6.6 Declaration of Competing Interests (supervisor is co-author of both the external dataset and the RL comparator method).
   **Why it matters** — The transfer experiment in Section 5.7 is described as testing "collection, route and time — not operator, and not radio access technology," which is honest, but the paper still uses the word "independent collection" in headline text (Section 1.6 uses similarly qualified language, but Table 5.11's caption and surrounding prose lean on "independently collected"). Combined with the RL baseline being reimplemented in-house from a method description of a paper from the same lab, rather than run with the original authors' code, there is a nontrivial risk that both the "external" test and the "weak baseline" result are shaped by shared assumptions/instrumentation rather than being a genuinely arm's-length check.
   **What would address it** — Seek a dataset and comparator implementation with no institutional overlap, and, failing that, ask the original RL-comparator authors to validate the reimplementation.

6. **Issue** — The causal account of *why* the alignment defect occurs (end-of-second aggregation, ~50–75 ms commit window) is validated only on external corpora the authors themselves downsampled, never on a native-rate re-export of the actual campaigns being predicted on.
   **Where** — Section 5.1: "it does not establish that XCAL's own one-hertz exporter aggregates that way, which remains inferred from its consequences and which only a native-rate re-export of these captures would settle; Section 5.13 carries that as a residual risk."
   **Why it matters** — The one-row lag "fix" applied throughout Chapter 5 is a plausible, evidence-consistent correction, but it is not a directly confirmed one for this dataset. If the true per-session commit latency varies (e.g., with cell load, device firmware, or across the "two academic terms" separating the campaigns), a single fixed one-row lag could over- or under-correct in ways the paper cannot detect without the native-rate ground truth it says it lacks. Since this correction is what turns the headline AUPRC from an inflated 0.600 into 0.179, its own evidentiary status deserves the same scrutiny the paper otherwise applies to the original leak.
   **What would address it** — Obtain even one native-rate (sub-second) re-export of a single campaign to directly confirm the write-timing rule on the actual instrument, rather than relying on inference from a different tool (G-NetTrack) and a downsampled third-party corpus (NUWiNS).

7. **Issue** — A load-bearing scope figure is stated but never reconciled with later numbers describing the same underlying limitation.
   **Where** — Section 1.5: "the measurement export is sampled at one hertz, which caps the fraction of handover events that can in principle be resolved at 90.5%," versus Section 3.6/4.10/5.5, which state the eligible-prediction-window ceiling as 64.2% at one second (35.8–36.4% unresolvable).
   **Why it matters** — These two numbers describe closely related concepts (how much of the event set the 1 Hz grid can, in principle, resolve) but differ by more than 25 percentage points with no visible arithmetic connecting them anywhere in the text. Given the number of quantities in this thesis that were revised between drafts, an unreconciled figure like this is exactly where a stale or superseded computation would hide, and it undercuts confidence in the "everything is regenerated from stage outputs" reproducibility claim of Appendix C.
   **What would address it** — Define the population and denominator behind the 90.5% figure explicitly and show how it relates to (or supersedes) the 64.2%/36.4% figures, or remove it.

### Minor concerns
- Table 5.2 reports the "lagged" one-second AUPRC as 0.179 ("this work"), while Table 5.3 reports the ostensibly identical alignment condition ("every export column (v2, as reported throughout)") as 0.160; the difference (tuned vs. fixed hyperparameters) is explained elsewhere but not cross-referenced at the point of the numbers, inviting a reader to compare the wrong cells.
- The reference list contains multiple unresolved editorial placeholders — "[Author list to be completed from the ACM record before submission]" (ref. 6), "[Full author list to be completed from the MDPI record before submission]" (ref. 15), "[confirm the version DOI before submission]" (ref. 38), "[Venue to be confirmed; a ResearchGate record exists]" (ref. 39) — indicating the manuscript is not yet in submission-ready form.
- Ref. [39], an unpublished, unrefereed in-house manuscript, is used as the paper's nearest comparator baseline; its methodological fidelity in reimplementation cannot be checked by a reader.
- Chapter 6 ("Demonstration of Outcome Based Education") and its associated appendices are capstone/accreditation material with no place in a journal submission and would need to be removed entirely before Q1 submission.
- Event counts drift slightly across tables without a pointer at first use (957 vs. 938 vs. 934–937 in Table A.2 per horizon); the 957→938 reconciliation is explained in Section 3.4, but the further per-horizon variation in Table A.2 is not explained inline.
- "Distribution-free risk control," "conformal risk control," and "conformal prediction" are used close to interchangeably in places; a reader unfamiliar with Angelopoulos et al. would benefit from one clear statement distinguishing the mean-risk guarantee actually used from coverage-style conformal prediction.
- The extracted thesis text shows heavy word-merging/typesetting artifacts in the front matter (likely a PDF-extraction issue rather than a defect of the original document), which should be verified against the source PDF before any of the above observations are treated as authorial errors rather than extraction noise.

### Verdict
**Major revision** — the leakage-audit contribution and the honesty about negative results are genuinely valuable, but the held-out campaign is not actually blind to the pipeline's defining preprocessing decision, key generalisation and risk-control claims rest on confounded or pseudo-replicated evidence from only four independent units, the causal mechanism behind the central correction is unconfirmed on the paper's own instrument, and the manuscript still contains submission-readiness defects (placeholder citations, an accreditation chapter) inconsistent with a Q1 journal target.

### Summary

This is a BSc capstone thesis asking whether the next LTE handover can be forecast ahead of the reactive Event‑A3 trigger, from four live drive‑test campaigns (4 sessions, 10,260 one‑hertz samples, 957 RRC‑decoded handover commands). The headline methodological finding is a timestamp‑alignment defect in the one‑hertz export (76% of handovers show post‑handover cell identity in the row stamped before the command), whose correction collapses the one‑second AUPRC from 0.600 to 0.179. On the corrected, leakage‑audited pipeline, a discrete‑time hazard model (LightGBM) reaches AUPRC 0.179 at 1 s (6.8% prevalence floor, 2.6× lift, AUROC 0.777) and 0.475 at 5 s, evaluated under leave‑one‑campaign‑out (the only protocol treated as yielding independent units, n=4). The thesis also reports a splitting-protocol ablation (random-row splitting inflates AUPRC by 48%), a coherent multi-horizon hazard formulation, and a distribution-free risk-control analysis that is explicitly reported as failing to establish exchangeability across campaigns, alongside corrected characterisations of the deployed A3 configuration and the ping-pong rate's sensitivity to definitional choices.

### Major concerns

1. **Issue** — The headline predictive-performance confidence intervals (e.g., AUPRC 0.179 [0.159, 0.204] at 1 s) are computed with exactly the block-bootstrap procedure that the thesis itself later proves is invalid on this data, yet this invalidated interval is retained as the reported uncertainty for the primary result throughout the abstract, Table 5.4, and the objectives discussion.
   **Where** — Table 5.4 ("Intervals are block-bootstrapped over 180s blocks... conditional on these four sessions"); contradicted by Section 5.3/5.4's own finding that "splitting by random 180-second blocks... still inflates it by 13%, because blocks of one continuous session are not independent of one another," and by the explicit retraction in Section 5.4: "resampling them deflates the standard error and manufactures a confidence interval narrower than the evidence supports... The claim is withdrawn."
   **Why it matters** — The retraction is applied only to the *paired arm-difference* comparisons in Section 5.4, not to the primary AUPRC/AUROC/ECE interval reported in Table 5.4 and repeated in the abstract and Chapter 7. But the same non-independence applies identically to that interval: it resamples non-independent 180 s blocks within held-out campaigns, so it understates uncertainty for the exact quantity (AUPRC 0.179) that is the thesis's central number. A reader is given a precise-looking interval ([0.159, 0.204]) for a result the authors elsewhere argue cannot be bounded that way with only 4 true independent units.
   **What would address it** — Either drop the block-bootstrap interval for Table 5.4 entirely and report only the per-campaign spread (as is already done, more honestly, in Table 5.10), or explicitly caveat every appearance of the block-bootstrap CI with the same disclaimer given in Section 5.4, so the reader does not treat [0.159, 0.204] as an honest precision statement.

2. **Issue** — The cross-campaign conformal risk-control result ("empirical holdout loss falling below α in 83% of 12 individual rotations") treats 12 calibrate/test rotations as if they were 12 roughly independent trials, when they are constructed as ordered pairs over only 4 underlying campaigns (4×3=12), so the effective sample size is 4, not 12.
   **Where** — Abstract; Section 5.5 ("Across the 12 cross-campaign rotations at α = 0.20... empirical loss falling below α in 83%, or 10 of 12, rotations"); Table 5.9.
   **Why it matters** — Because every rotation reuses one of only 4 campaigns as either the calibration or the test set, the 12 outcomes are heavily correlated (pseudoreplicated): a single unusually well- or poorly-behaved campaign can dominate several rotations at once. Reporting "83%" implies a resolution the underlying data cannot support, and risks being read by an operator or a future reviewer as a more reliable empirical success rate than 4 genuinely independent trials would justify. The thesis is careful about this exact issue everywhere else (explicitly refusing p-values from n=4), which makes the uncritical "83% of 12 rotations" framing here an inconsistency in the applied statistical standard.
   **What would address it** — State explicitly that the 12 rotations derive from only 4 independent campaigns and are not independent replicates; report the result broken out by which campaign served as calibration source (so the reader can see whether the 83% is driven by one or two campaigns), rather than pooling into a single percentage.

3. **Issue** — The "primary model" (LightGBM) reported throughout the abstract, contributions, and headline tables is selected from a leaderboard of 7 learners whose confidence intervals mostly overlap, but no pre-registration of LightGBM as the intended primary model prior to seeing results is stated, so the headline number carries an unquantified winner's-curse-style optimism from implicit selection.
   **Where** — Section 5.2 / Table 5.5 ("LightGBM is first at 0.179, MLP second at 0.173... the intervals of 10 of the arms overlap the leader's... The ordering of the top arms is not a finding of this thesis"); Section 4.7 designates LightGBM as "the primary model" without stating when that designation was fixed relative to the comparison.
   **Why it matters** — The thesis correctly disclaims that the *ranking* is not a finding, but it does not extend that caution to the *magnitude* of the reported headline AUPRC, which is still the single largest of the 7 point estimates and is the number carried into the abstract, objectives, and conclusion. If "primary model" was chosen after seeing Table 5.5 (which the freeze description in Section 3.2/5.2 does not clearly rule out for horizon-specific model selection, as opposed to the feature/formulation freeze), the reported effect size is the maximum of 7 correlated estimates rather than a single pre-specified test statistic.
   **What would address it** — State explicitly when and how LightGBM was designated primary relative to the comparison of Table 5.5 (before or after computing it), and, if after, report the headline number either as an average over learners or with an explicit multiplicity-adjusted interval rather than the raw maximum.

4. **Issue** — Numerous strong descriptive claims (A3 conversion rates, ping-pong rate across 9 definitional cells, the 76%/86.2%/93.2% contamination percentages, the 96%/2% attribution of AUPRC loss to feature blocks in Table 5.3) are reported as point estimates with no uncertainty interval, even though they are used to support mechanistic and normative conclusions ("the separation... survives all three [definitions] and is widest under the strictest").
   **Where** — Table 5.3 ("accounting for 95.8% of the reduction"), Table 5.14, Table 5.15/5.16, Section 5.1's contamination percentages.
   **Why it matters** — Some of these proportions are computed on small subgroups (e.g., n=15 boundary-crossing handovers, n=211 residual cases, n=93 inter-frequency handovers in Table 5.14) where sampling variability could be substantial, but the thesis reports them to one decimal place as if exact. This is inconsistent with the appropriately cautious statistical posture the thesis takes elsewhere (e.g., explicitly refusing significance tests on n=4 campaigns) and could mislead a reader into over-trusting fine-grained percentage differences computed on small n.
   **What would address it** — Add binomial confidence intervals (or at minimum, denominators alongside every percentage, which is mostly but not universally done) for proportions computed on subgroups below roughly n=50, particularly in Tables 5.3, 5.14, and the boundary-crossing evidence in Table A.6.

5. **Issue** — The thesis's evaluation protocol involves an extremely large number of researcher degrees of freedom exercised after all data were collected (180 s block length, 60 s purge, 10 s burst/quiet cutoff, 2 s blanking window, choice of 15 equal-mass calibration bins, choice of horizons), and while a sensitivity table (A.5) is provided, the thesis's own sensitivity analysis shows at least one result (the blocked-vs-LOCO gap) straddles zero and is explicitly "not established... in either direction," yet this same blocked protocol is elsewhere used as a practical recommendation ("which is what makes it a usable protocol when only one session is available").
   **Where** — Section 5.13 ("Post-hoc windows"); Table A.5; Section 5.3.
   **Why it matters** — Recommending the blocked+purge protocol as a practical substitute for leave-one-campaign-out, while simultaneously reporting that its own sensitivity analysis cannot establish the sign of its bias relative to LOCO, is an internally inconsistent recommendation: the thesis cannot both certify the protocol as "usable" and disclaim knowledge of whether it over- or under-estimates performance.
   **What would address it** — Either withdraw the practical recommendation to use blocked+purge splitting when only one session is available, or qualify it explicitly as "direction of bias unknown from this data" rather than implying it is a safe substitute.

6. **Issue** — No correction, or even discussion, is given for the number of statistical claims being tested informally across the thesis's many tables (7 learners × 5 horizons × 4 splitting protocols × 5+ calibration arms × 4 campaigns), beyond the single acknowledgment that "with four independent units... no [multiplicity correction] would be informative."
   **Where** — Section 4.7 (tuning-budget discussion); pervasive across Chapter 5.
   **Why it matters** — The "no correction possible with n=4" argument is reasonable for the specific paired-campaign comparisons the thesis restricts itself to, but it is used to justify skipping multiplicity consideration everywhere, including for comparisons that do not rely on the 4-campaign unit (e.g., the 22-cell definitional grid for ping-pong in Figure 5.15, the many single-feature AUROC comparisons in Table 5.12, or the ablation grid in Table 5.3). These have larger effective sample sizes where at least a qualitative acknowledgment of multiple comparisons (e.g., that 22 grid cells were computed and one convenient contrast is highlighted) would be appropriate.
   **What would address it** — Distinguish explicitly between comparisons genuinely limited by n=4 (where the "no correction possible" argument holds) and comparisons computed on the full row-level dataset (n in the thousands), and address multiplicity for the latter category even qualitatively.

7. **Issue** — Reproducibility of the reported statistics is deferred: code and derived data are "released on acceptance," meaning none of the specific numbers, contamination audits, or bootstrap procedures can currently be independently verified.
   **Where** — Section 7.3 ("Release of code and data"); Appendix C.
   **Why it matters** — Given how central small-sample statistical judgment calls are to this thesis's contribution (which arm counts as "coherent," which window length is used, how the 12 rotations are constructed), independent verification is unusually important here, more so than in a typical prediction paper, and currently impossible.
   **What would address it** — Release the derived frames and pipeline code alongside submission (or to reviewers under embargo) rather than contingent on acceptance, particularly the alignment-audit script and the conformal risk-control rotation construction.

### Minor concerns

- Section 2.3 contains a verbatim duplicated paragraph ("The narrow claim the audit supports, and the one made in this thesis, is therefore the following...") appearing twice in immediate succession — looks like a drafting/merge artifact rather than intentional repetition.
- Several reference entries are marked with editorial placeholders not resolved before this version ("[Author list to be completed from the ACM record before submission]," "[Full author list to be completed from the MDPI record before submission]," "[Venue to be confirmed]," "[Volume, issue and page range to be confirmed]") — these should not remain in a submission-ready manuscript.
- The "independent" collection used for generalisation in Section 5.7 is disclosed as sharing supervisor/department/instrument/operator with the primary campaigns (Section 6.6 COI declaration); this is handled honestly but the word "independent" is still used loosely in a few places (e.g., Table 5.11 caption) despite the text's own downgrading of the claim.
- Table 5.9's "Feasible rot." and "Bound met" column semantics are not clearly defined in the table itself and require cross-referencing Section 5.5's prose to interpret correctly.
- Given the thesis format (embedded OBE/course-outcome chapter, cost budget in BDT), substantial restructuring would be needed before this reads as a standalone journal submission; Chapter 6 in particular would need to be removed entirely.

### Verdict

**Major revision** — the core contribution (the alignment audit and the honest, self-correcting statistical posture) is genuine and unusually rigorous for this scale of study, but the inconsistent application of the authors' own uncertainty-quantification standard to the headline result (Concern 1) and the pseudoreplication in the cross-campaign conformal evaluation (Concern 2) must be fixed before the reported precision of the central claims can be trusted.

SEED: b4e19f7c2d8a0361f5e9c7b2a8d40e16 LENS: Statistical methodology (int("b4",16)=180, 180 mod 6 = 0) STANCE: Skeptical-but-fair (int("e1",16)=225, 225 mod 3 = 0) (arXiv lookup attempted twice — `conformal risk control wireless network exchangeability calibration` and `conformal risk control small sample calibration exchangeability` — both failed with a proxy connection error unrelated to query content; continuing from the paper text alone per the fallback rule.) --- # Review (Reviewer: delta) ### Summary This EEE bachelor's thesis asks whether the next LTE handover can be forecast from handset-observable measurements, at multiple horizons, with a stated statistical guarantee. Using four drive-test campaigns (957 signalling-confirmed handovers, 10,260 one-hertz samples) on a single commercial LTE operator, the authors first uncover and correct a severe timestamp-alignment defect in their own 1 Hz export (a row stamped before a handover command already reflects the post-handover serving cell in 76% of cases), which collapses their one-second AUPRC from 0.600 to 0.179 once corrected. On the corrected data, they pose multi-horizon prediction as discrete-time survival (hazard-based, guaranteeing monotonicity across horizons) and report LightGBM as the best of seven learners (AUPRC 0.179 at 1s / 0.475 at 5s against prevalence floors of 6.8%/26.1%), compare four data-splitting protocols (showing random-row splitting inflates AUPRC by 48% relative to leave-one-campaign-out), and apply conformal risk control to bound miss rates, while explicitly flagging that the cross-campaign exchangeability assumption needed for the bound to be a real guarantee is not established. The headline contribution is framed as a leakage-audited measurement/evaluation framework rather than a deployable predictor. ### Major concerns 1. **Issue** — The central conformal risk-control result is calibrated and evaluated on only 4 independent units (campaigns), which is far below the sample size needed for any of the paper's own feasibility-floor arithmetic to mean what it claims, and the "83% of 12 rotations" statistic conflates dependent rotations as if they added information. **Where** — Section 4.10 (Equation 4.12), Section 5.5, Table 5.9, and the abstract's claim "empirical holdout loss falling below α in 83% of 12 individual rotations." **Why it matters** — With only 4 campaigns, a leave-one-campaign-out conformal calibration has at most 4 truly distinct held-out evaluations; the "12 individual rotations" figure is not defined anywhere precisely enough to know whether it double-counts the same 4 campaigns under different (α, threshold) settings or genuinely draws 12 exchangeable calibration/test splits. If it is the former (which the surrounding text strongly suggests, since block counts are given as n ∈ {8,14,15,20} per campaign), then "83%" is a descriptive tally over highly dependent outcomes, not evidence of coverage frequency in any statistical sense — it cannot be interpreted as an empirical false-coverage rate the way the abstract's phrasing invites a reader to do. The paper is careful in prose to say "results are descriptive," but the number is still presented prominently (abstract, Section 5.5, Table 5.9, Chapter 7) in a way that borrows the rhetorical weight of a validation statistic. A statistically literate reader will ask: descriptive of what population, and with what standard error? None is given, and none can be meaningfully given with n=4. **What would address it** — Either drop the "83% of 12 rotations" framing from the abstract/conclusion (keep it, if anywhere, buried in Section 5.5 with an explicit statement that it has no inferential content), or replace it with the actual per-campaign realized losses (4 numbers) with no aggregate percentage at all, since that is the only quantity for which independence is defended elsewhere in the same thesis (Section 5.4's use of "4 of 4 campaigns" as the only defensible comparison unit). The inconsistency — treating 4 units as the only legitimate unit for AUPRC comparisons in Section 5.4, but then computing an aggregate "83% of 12" statistic for the conformal result in Section 5.5 — is itself a methodological contradiction that should be resolved. 2. **Issue** — No correction for multiple comparisons or selective reporting is applied across the very large number of comparisons the thesis runs (7 learners × 5 horizons × 4 splitting protocols × several calibration arms × several ablations × several ping-pong definitional grids), and while the authors are commendably explicit that "no multiplicity correction is applied" (Section 4.7), the justification given ("with four independent units none would be informative") does not follow — the multiplicity problem here is not about the 4 campaign units, it is about the dozens of researcher-degree-of-freedom comparisons (splitting windows, blank windows, burst cutoffs, feature-block ablations) that are each reported as a single point estimate. **Where** — Section 4.7 ("Nomultiplicitycorrectionisapplied..."), Table A.5 (sensitivity of four post-hoc windows), Section 5.8 (burst/quiet cutoff), Section 5.9 (three counting units for A3 conversion), Section 5.10 (nine-cell definitional grid for ping-pong). **Why it matters** — The paper's own Table A.5 shows that varying the purge window alone swings the blocked-vs-LOCO gap from -5.6% to +3.7%, and it explicitly says this "straddles zero" and is "not established... in either direction." That is an honest admission, but it also means several other single-point sensitivity results reported without a corresponding interval (e.g., the burst/quiet cutoff ordering, the quiet-lift figures in Section 5.8, the per-profile A3 conversion rates in Table 5.14) are subject to the same researcher-degrees-of-freedom risk without the same caveat attached. The thesis is inconsistent about which post-hoc choices get a sensitivity analysis and which do not. **What would address it** — Extend the Table A.5-style sensitivity sweep to every post-hoc threshold used in a headline claim (the burst/quiet split, the A3 report-conversion window, the ping-pong return window grid already exists but is not accompanied by an uncertainty statement on top of the definitional grid itself), and state explicitly, next to each headline number, whether its robustness to the underlying choice has been checked. 3. **Issue** — The paper reports point estimates for calibration error (ECE) and single "confidence intervals" from a block bootstrap that the paper itself has already shown (Section 5.3) understates variance because blocks are not independent, yet it continues to use exactly this bootstrap for the primary AUPRC intervals in Table 5.4 and Table 5.5, only switching to the (correct, but very coarse) 4-campaign spread for the paired hazard-vs-control comparison in Section 5.4. **Where** — Table 5.4, Table 5.5 (block-bootstrap CIs) versus Section 5.4/Table 5.8 (where the block-bootstrap interval is explicitly withdrawn as "manufactur[ing] a confidence interval narrower than the evidence supports"). **Why it matters** — This is a direct internal inconsistency: the authors prove in one section that the block-bootstrap CI is invalid because blocks are correlated (Section 5.3's finding that block-splitting itself inflates AUPRC by 13%), then use that same invalid interval-generation method for the primary performance table (Table 5.4) that a reader is most likely to cite (e.g., "AUPRC 0.179, 95% CI [0.159, 0.204]"). If the block bootstrap is not trustworthy for testing a hazard-vs-control difference, it is not trustworthy for characterizing uncertainty in the headline AUPRC either — the same non-independence applies to both. **What would address it** — Either relabel every block-bootstrap interval in the thesis (not just Table 5.8) as "within-campaign, non-inferential spread" consistently, or drop the false appearance of precision in Table 5.4/5.5 and report only the 4-campaign range there too, matching the standard the authors apply to themselves in Section 5.4. 4. **Issue** — The nested nested hyperparameter search (20 trials × 7 learners × 4 folds × 3 seeds) is run on a dataset with roughly 600 positive rows at the 1-second horizon, and while the authors note this is "a large search relative to roughly six hundred positive rows," they do not quantify the risk that the search itself, even though it cannot see the held-out campaign, can still overfit to the *idiosyncrasies of the training-campaign mixture* in a way that a 4-fold rotation cannot detect, because each "outer fold" reuses the same 3 remaining campaigns for both search and final fit.
**Where** — Section 4.7 ("Every arm receives the same tuning budget..."), Section 5.2. **Why it matters** — With only 3 campaigns available for training+tuning in each outer fold, the 20-trial random search selects hyperparameters using the same 3 sessions it then trains the final model on (unless a further internal split is used, which is not described precisely — the text says the search is "scored on a calibration block held out of that fold's training data," which is a within-training-campaigns split, not a fourth independent unit). This means hyperparameter selection is optimizing against exactly the same 3-campaign idiosyncrasies that the final model is fit on, so held-out AUPRC could still be inflated relative to what a genuinely new corridor would show, even though "no held-out campaign is ever scored during a search" is technically true. **What would address it** — State explicitly how many independent units back the internal tuning split (it sounds like it is a temporal/row-level split within the 3 training campaigns, which reintroduces exactly the near-duplicate-row risk that Section 5.3 spends a whole section warning about), and, if so, flag this as a residual, not fully eliminated, leakage risk in Section 5.13's threats-to-validity list (it currently is not mentioned there). ### Minor concerns - Table 2.1 and the surrounding audit narrative round-trip through overlapping claims ("Reports calibration... 0/22" appears identically twice at the end of Section 2.3, verbatim, suggesting a copy-paste duplication artifact in the manuscript). - The abstract states "an empirical hypothesis falsified by none of the 15 handovers here whose execution crosses the boundary" — "falsified by none" is an odd double negative for "confirmed by all 15"; given n=15, this should be stated with appropriate humility about sample size rather than as if it strongly corroborates the mechanism. - Reference [15] (Amirova et al.) and [39] (the RL comparator) both carry bracketed reproducibility notes ("Full author list to be completed," "Venue to be confirmed") that should not remain in a document being reviewed as final — these read as unresolved TODOs in the reference list. - Table 5.9's row for α=0.05 uses an asterisked "0.000*" / "100%*" combination that is explained only in a dense footnote; this table would benefit from plain-language annotation given how much of the thesis's core "boundary result" contribution rests on it. - The n for cross-campaign calibration units is reported inconsistently as "12 individual rotations" (abstract, Section 5.5) versus "n ∈ {8,14,15,20}" (four values, Table 5.9) without a clear one-line explanation of how four campaigns produce twelve rotations; this should be spelled out explicitly the first time either number appears. - Minor arithmetic self-consistency point: Table 3.2 lists 957 total handover commands, but the abstract and multiple in-text passages alternate between "938" (quality-controlled) and "957" (raw decoded) without always flagging which is in use in a given sentence (e.g., Figure 3.1's caption "N=938" versus Section 1.2's "957 signalling-confirmed handover commands"). ### Verdict **Major revision** — the underlying leakage/alignment audit is a genuinely valuable and unusually honest methodological contribution, but the statistical treatment of uncertainty is internally inconsistent (a bootstrap the authors themselves discredit is still used for the headline table), and the conformal risk-control result's "83% of 12 rotations" statistic is presented with more inferential weight in the abstract than 4 independent campaigns can support.

# Meta-Review

**Paper:** Conformalized Discrete-Time Hazard Modeling for Multi-Horizon Handover Forecasting in Cellular Networks
**Reviewers:** alfa, bravo, charlie, delta (4 independent panelists)

## Per-reviewer verdicts

- **alfa** — Major revision: the alignment-audit contribution is strong, but the primary predictive and risk-control numbers are defended with confidence intervals the paper's own Section 5.3 analysis shows to be anti-conservative when applied to this data's block structure, and that inconsistency must be resolved before the quantitative claims can be taken at face value.
- **bravo** — Major revision: the leakage-audit contribution and the honesty about negative results are genuinely valuable, but the held-out campaign is not actually blind to the pipeline's defining preprocessing decision, key generalisation and risk-control claims rest on confounded or pseudo-replicated evidence from only four independent units, the causal mechanism behind the central correction is unconfirmed on the paper's own instrument, and the manuscript still contains submission-readiness defects.
- **charlie** — Major revision: the core contribution (the alignment audit and the honest, self-correcting statistical posture) is genuine and unusually rigorous for this scale of study, but the inconsistent application of the authors' own uncertainty-quantification standard to the headline result and the pseudoreplication in the cross-campaign conformal evaluation must be fixed before the reported precision of the central claims can be trusted.
- **delta** — Major revision: the underlying leakage/alignment audit is a genuinely valuable and unusually honest methodological contribution, but the statistical treatment of uncertainty is internally inconsistent, and the conformal risk-control result's "83% of 12 rotations" statistic is presented with more inferential weight in the abstract than four independent campaigns can support.

## Common concerns

1. **Block-bootstrap confidence intervals are internally inconsistent with the paper's own findings.** The headline AUPRC/AUROC/ECE intervals in Tables 5.4–5.5 are computed with the same 180-second block-bootstrap procedure that Section 5.3/5.4 independently proves to be anti-conservative on this data (block-splitting itself inflates one-second AUPRC by 13%), and Section 5.4 explicitly withdraws a paired-comparison claim on that basis — but the identical mechanism is left unflagged everywhere it produces the paper's most-cited number.
   Raised by: **alfa, charlie, delta**.
   Strongest formulation (charlie): *"If the block bootstrap is not trustworthy for testing a hazard-vs-control difference, it is not trustworthy for characterizing uncertainty in the headline AUPRC either — the same non-independence applies to both."*

2. **The conformal risk-control "83% of 12 rotations" statistic pseudoreplicates four independent campaigns as if they were twelve.** Because every rotation reuses one of only four campaigns as calibration or test set, the twelve outcomes are correlated through shared campaign identity, so the reported percentage carries a resolution the underlying data cannot support — and does so in the abstract and conclusion, not just deep in Section 5.5.
   Raised by: **alfa, bravo, charlie, delta** (unanimous).
   Strongest formulation (delta): *"'83%' is a descriptive tally over highly dependent outcomes, not evidence of coverage frequency in any statistical sense — it cannot be interpreted as an empirical false-coverage rate the way the abstract's phrasing invites a reader to do."*

3. **The held-out campaign is not a genuinely blind generalization test.** The one-row alignment/lag correction that defines the entire feature pipeline was derived by pooling contamination evidence across all four campaigns — including the campaign later reported as "held out" for the leave-one-campaign-out evaluation — so what survives as a clean test is the model's hyperparameters, not the measurement pipeline that determines what the model sees.
   Raised by: **alfa, bravo**.
   Strongest formulation (bravo): *"A skeptic should ask: would the audit have concluded 'lag by exactly one row' if only Campaigns 1–3 had been available? The paper does not show this."*

4. **Small-subgroup point estimates are reported without uncertainty, at odds with the paper's own cautious standard elsewhere.** Percentages computed on subgroups as small as n=15 (the boundary-crossing falsification test) or n=93–291 (various contamination and feature-block breakdowns) are stated to one decimal place as if exact, while the same thesis explicitly refuses significance testing at n=4 campaigns.
   Raised by: **alfa, charlie**.

5. **Reference list contains unresolved bibliographic placeholders.** Multiple entries carry literal editorial TODOs — incomplete author lists, unconfirmed DOIs/venues/volume-page ranges — inconsistent with a submission-ready manuscript, and one of them ([38]) underlies the Section 5.7 generalization claim.
   Raised by: **alfa, bravo, charlie, delta** (unanimous; flagged as a minor/administrative issue by all four, not a major concern in itself).

6. **Chapter 6 (Outcome-Based Education mapping) is capstone-accreditation boilerplate with no place in a journal submission.** All four reviewers independently flagged this chapter, and the associated appendices, for removal before any journal-track version of the manuscript.
   Raised by: **alfa, bravo, charlie, delta** (unanimous minor concern).

7. **Handover/event counts drift across chapters without consistent flagging.** The raw decoded count (957), the quality-controlled count (938), and further per-horizon counts (934–937) are used somewhat interchangeably across tables and prose.
   Raised by: **alfa, bravo, delta**.

## Unique concerns

- **alfa** — The claim that no prior wireless conformal-prediction study addresses a mobility-management case rests on an unspecified, undocumented literature screen, unlike the transparent 108→22 screen the same thesis uses for the handover-prediction literature in Section 2.3.
- **bravo** — The "freeze" of modelling decisions prior to the held-out campaign is attested only by the authors' own private version history, with no independent or third-party timestamp.
- **bravo** — The generalization claim (Objective O4) confounds corridor and speed regime, since the held-out campaign differs from the others on both axes simultaneously — a confound the thesis itself explicitly acknowledges for a different analysis (ping-pong) but not here.
- **bravo** — The two external-validity checks (the "independent" public dataset and the RL comparator baseline) share supervisor, department, instrument, and operator lineage with the primary study, which sits uneasily with "independent collection" language used in headline text.
- **bravo** — The causal mechanism proposed for the alignment defect (end-of-second export aggregation) is validated only on external, downsampled corpora and never confirmed on a native-rate re-export of the actual campaigns being predicted on.
- **bravo** — A stated 90.5% event-resolvability ceiling is never reconciled with a different, materially lower 64.2% eligible-prediction-window figure used elsewhere for what appears to be the same underlying 1 Hz sampling limitation.
- **charlie** — LightGBM is designated the "primary model" from a seven-learner comparison whose confidence intervals mostly overlap, with no stated pre-registration of that choice, risking winner's-curse-style optimism in the headline effect size.
- **charlie** — The blocked+purge splitting protocol is recommended as a practical leave-one-campaign-out substitute even though the paper's own sensitivity analysis (Table A.5) cannot establish the direction of its bias relative to LOCO.
- **charlie** — No multiplicity correction is applied to the large number of full-dataset comparisons (splitting windows, cutoffs, definitional grids), conflating this with the separate and valid argument that no correction is informative at the n=4-campaign level.
- **delta** — The internal hyperparameter-tuning split is drawn from within the same three training campaigns used for the final fit rather than a fourth independent unit, so tuning may leak training-campaign idiosyncrasies that the leave-one-campaign-out rotation cannot detect.

## Ranking

1. **charlie** — Most systematically exposes internally inconsistent statistical standards across multiple parts of the paper (bootstrap CI misuse, conformal pseudoreplication, post-hoc primary-model selection, unaddressed multiplicity, deferred reproducibility) with precise textual anchors in each case; broadest coverage of concerns that go to the core validity of the headline numbers.
2. **delta** — Independently converges on the same bootstrap and pseudoreplication flaws as charlie via a different reading of the text, and contributes one genuinely new, non-overlapping concern (internal tuning-split leakage) that no other reviewer identified.
3. **bravo** — Raises the single most structurally consequential critique in the panel (the held-out campaign is not blind to the pipeline-defining alignment correction) and layers on five further largely non-overlapping design concerns (freeze provenance, confounded regime, COI-adjacent external validity, unconfirmed causal mechanism, scope-figure mismatch); very high per-concern novelty, somewhat less tightly focused on the statistical core than charlie or delta.
4. **alfa** — Corroborates the two most-repeated concerns in the panel (held-out contamination, bootstrap-CI inconsistency) and adds one genuinely novel point (the undocumented literature-screen claim), but contributes comparatively less new ground once bravo's and charlie/delta's findings are on the table.

## Verdict synthesis

**Major revision.** All four reviewers reached this verdict independently and there is no disagreement to arbitrate. Two systemic issues were found by every reviewer working from the paper text alone and via different routes: the block-bootstrap confidence intervals attached to the headline AUPRC/AUROC/ECE figures use exactly the resampling procedure the thesis's own Section 5.3/5.4 shows to be anti-conservative on this data, and the cross-campaign conformal result ("83% of 12 rotations") pseudoreplicates outcomes from only four independent campaigns while being reported with the rhetorical weight of a validation statistic. Both are fixable without new data collection — by re-expressing uncertainty using the 4-campaign spread the paper already reports honestly elsewhere (e.g., Table 5.10), consistent with the standard the authors apply to themselves when they withdraw the Section 5.4 paired-comparison claim. The next most serious issue, raised independently by two reviewers, is that the leave-one-campaign-out evaluation's "held-out" campaign is not blind to the alignment-audit correction that defines the entire feature pipeline, since that correction was derived from evidence pooled across all four campaigns; this weakens, without invalidating, the paper's generalization claim and should be either reframed or re-tested with the pipeline frozen on three campaigns only. None of the panel disputes that the alignment-audit finding itself — the discovery that a one-hertz export artifact inflates apparent AUPRC by more than 3× — is a genuine, well-corroborated, and independently valuable contribution; the consensus is that the predictive and risk-control claims built on top of it are currently defended with more statistical confidence than the paper's own n=4-campaign evidence base, by the paper's own logic, supports. Administrative issues (unresolved reference placeholders, the accreditation-chapter content) are unanimous but straightforward to fix before any journal submission.
